elements.text: American Airlines maintenance personnel used an inappropriate manual engine-start procedure
Uncommanded opening of the left engine air turbine starter valve
Left engine fire
Flight crew interrupted an emergency checklist to perform nonessential tasks, prolonging the fire
Deficiencies in American Airlines’ Continuing Analysis and Surveillance System program
Maintenance personnel did not clean the air turbine starter valve-air filter in accordance with C check procedures
Filter element disintegrated, allowing the end cap to become free and block air flow
Maintenance troubleshooting incorrectly focused on the ATSV and wiring due to intermittent conditions and lack of guidance
Maintenance personnel used an unapproved procedure involving a prying device, bending the internal pin in the override button
Bent internal pin in the ATSV override button caused uncommanded opening during high-power conditions
Failed air turbine starter allowed hot airstream/particles to flow into the nacelle, providing an ignition source
Combustible fluid was available in the engine
Pilots failed to immediately detect or respond to the ATSV-Open light due to its design and perceived low urgency
Pilots failed to properly allocate tasks and manage workload, adversely affecting checklist execution
Interruption of the Engine Fire/Damage/Separation checklist led to loss of hydraulic pressure and nose gear failure
First officer lacked understanding of the relationship between pneumatic crossfeed and engine fire handles, reintroducing fuel to the engine
Casual cockpit atmosphere eroded safety margins and set a precedent for poor responses
Flight attendants did not relay pertinent information to the captain in accordance with guidance
Boeing and PTI inspection criteria for the ATSV-air filter are inadequate to detect early-stage fatigue fractures
American Airlines maintenance procedures were not in accordance with written manuals
Flight crewmembers were properly certificated and qualified
No evidence of preexisting medical or physical conditions affecting performance
Captain's sleep apnea was effectively treated and did not affect performance
No evidence of flight crew fatigue
Accident airplane was properly certificated and equipped
Weight and balance were within prescribed limits
ATC did not facilitate emergency radio frequency, but it did not impede ARFF efforts
Coupling ATSV-Open light with Master Caution might increase detection but has unintended consequences
Captain's decision to go around was reasonable given altitude and time constraints
Captain's decision not to evacuate was appropriate as fire was not severe and ARFF was responding
Incident commander's decision to deplane passengers was prudent
Improved pilot training methods would help develop skills for multiple failures
Operational procedures for evacuation configuration would help expedite evacuation
No preexisting indicators in training or performance histories explained poor performance
